chapter_summary:
As your game grows, you'll accumulate many GameObjects, each with its own set of components. To manage this complexity, Unity uses **Scenes**. A Scene is essentially a single level, menu, or segment of your game. It's a container that holds all the GameObjects, cameras, lights, and environments that exist together at a particular moment in your game. Think of a scene as a unique stage for a play; each stage has its own set, props, and lighting, distinct from other stages.

When you start a new Unity project, you begin with a default, empty scene. You can create new scenes by going to `File > New Scene` and save them via `File > Save Scene As...`. Scenes are saved as `.unity` files in your Project window. You can have multiple scenes in your project, but only one can be active and loaded at a time during gameplay (though Unity does support additive scene loading for more advanced scenarios, where multiple scenes can be loaded simultaneously). Switching between scenes is a fundamental aspect of game flow, moving from a main menu scene to a game level scene, or between different levels. This is typically handled programmatically using `SceneManager.LoadScene()` from the `UnityEngine.SceneManagement` namespace. It's crucial to add all scenes that your game will use to the "Build Settings" (`File > Build Settings > Scenes In Build`) so they are included when you build your game.

While scenes organize the larger structure of your game, **Prefabs** are the solution for organizing and reusing individual GameObjects or groups of GameObjects. A Prefab is a pre-configured GameObject stored as an asset in your Project window. It's a template from which you can create multiple instances in any scene. Imagine you're building a city and need hundreds of identical streetlights. Instead of manually configuring each streetlight GameObject (adding a pole, a light source, a specific material, and a script) every time, you create one perfect streetlight, turn it into a Prefab, and then drag and drop instances of that Prefab wherever you need them.

The primary benefits of Prefabs are:
1.  **Reusability:** Create once, use many times.
2.  **Consistency:** All instances of a Prefab share the same properties defined in the original Prefab asset.
3.  **Efficiency:** Changes made to the original Prefab asset are automatically propagated to all its instances across all scenes in your project. This is a massive time-saver for iterative development. For example, if you decide to change the color of your streetlight, you only modify the Prefab asset, and all 100 streetlights in your city update instantly.

Creating a Prefab is simple:
1.  Configure a GameObject (or a hierarchy of GameObjects) in your Scene view exactly how you want it.
2.  Drag that GameObject from the Hierarchy window into the Project window (typically into a dedicated `Prefabs` folder).
3.  The original GameObject in the Hierarchy will turn blue, indicating it's now an instance of a Prefab. The new Prefab asset will appear in your Project window.

Once you have a Prefab, you can drag instances of it from the Project window into any scene. Each instance is linked to the original Prefab asset. You can modify individual properties of a Prefab instance in the Scene view or Inspector (these are called **Overrides**), and they will be highlighted in bold in the Inspector. For example, you might want one streetlight instance to be slightly rotated or positioned differently. These overrides are local to that specific instance and do not affect the original Prefab asset or other instances.

If you make changes to an instance and want those changes to apply to the original Prefab (and thus to all other instances), you can use the "Overrides" dropdown in the Inspector of the instance and select "Apply All." Conversely, "Revert All" will discard local overrides and reset the instance back to the Prefab's original state.

Unity also introduces **Prefab Variants**, which allow you to create a Prefab that inherits from another Prefab. This is incredibly powerful for creating variations of a base object without duplicating the entire asset. For example, you could have a "BaseEnemy" Prefab, and then create "MeleeEnemy" and "RangedEnemy" Prefab Variants. The variants inherit all properties from "BaseEnemy" but can have their own specific overrides (e.g., different weapon models, different AI scripts). If you update the "BaseEnemy" (e.g., change its health script), those changes automatically propagate to both "MeleeEnemy" and "RangedEnemy" variants, unless overridden. This hierarchical Prefab system is a cornerstone of scalable game development.

Common mistakes with Prefabs include:
*   Forgetting to apply changes from an instance back to the Prefab, leading to inconsistencies.
*   Modifying a Prefab instance expecting it to create a new Prefab, instead of just creating an override.
*   Not understanding that Prefabs are assets in the Project window, and instances are in the Hierarchy.

By effectively using Scenes to structure your game's flow and Prefabs to manage reusable game elements, you lay a solid foundation for building complex and maintainable projects.

screens.title: Understanding Scenes and Prefabs
screens.subtitle: Organizing levels, reusing objects, and building scalable game content

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn two foundational Unity concepts that keep projects manageable: Scenes and Prefabs. Scenes act as containers for all objects, cameras, lights, and level data — the distinct stages of your game. Prefabs are reusable assets, templates of GameObjects or hierarchies you can place many times across scenes. Together they separate concerns: scenes organize where things live and when they load; prefabs define what repeatable things look and behave like. For example, a level scene holds terrain, lighting, and enemy placements; a streetlight or health pack becomes a Prefab so you can place many consistent copies quickly. You'll practice creating a new scene, saving it as a. unity file, adding it to Build Settings, making a simple collectible GameObject into a Prefab, and instantiating multiple instances both in the editor and at runtime. We'll also cover overrides and Prefab Variants so you can make controlled changes to instances or create specialized child templates that inherit updates. By the end, you should understand why this separation is essential for scaling projects and reducing repetitive work, and you'll have a hands-on checklist to start building reusable content in your own game.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use Scenes to organize game flow and Prefabs to make reusable templates — together they enable scalable, maintainable Unity projects.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives focus on practical skills you will use every day in Unity. First, you will explain what Scenes are and how they structure your game, including saving scenes as. unity files and ensuring they are included in Build Settings. Second, you will create, save, and load scenes programmatically and from the editor, so you can drive game flow. Third, you will define a Prefab and create one from a configured GameObject so that you can reuse assets without duplication. Fourth, you will manage Prefab instances, author overrides, and use Apply All or Revert All to keep instances consistent or intentionally different. Each objective is framed so you can practice immediately: create a scene, author a prefab, place several instances, change one instance, and then apply or revert changes. These skills matter because they reduce repetitive work, keep scenes consistent, and let teams scale level design without breaking shared templates. As you work through the lab, check these objectives off by performing the specific actions described. By the end you should be able to explain the why, show the how, and fix common mistakes.

screens.title: What is a Scene?
screens.subtitle: A Scene as a container for runtime state and level content

narration.text: A Scene is a self-contained container that holds all the GameObjects, cameras, lights, and environment elements that make up a single playable level or UI screen. Think of it as a stage with props and lighting, where only the objects placed on that stage exist while the scene is active. For example, your Main Menu scene may include UI canvases and a camera, while Level1 contains terrain, enemies, and player spawns. This separation matters because it limits memory and organizes authoring: you edit a smaller, focused set of objects rather than one giant scene. A common misconception is that scenes are the same as builds — they are not. Scenes are editor and runtime containers stored as. unity files, and you must add them to Build Settings to include them in the final game. Another misconception is that only one scene can be loaded at a time: Unity supports additive loading for advanced workflows where multiple scenes share content, like separating lighting from level geometry. Key actions you will practice: create a new scene, save it as a. unity file, and add it to Scenes In Build so it packages with your game. Consider: what elements in your project should be isolated into their own scene to make iteration faster?

keyIdea.title: Scene definition
keyIdea.text: A Scene is a level or state container in Unity; save scenes as .unity files and manage which scenes appear in a build.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a Scene?
Definition

Scene = Stage

A Scene groups the objects that exist together at a particular moment. It’s saved as a .unity file and represents a single level or UI state.

Why it matters
  • Limits memory usage by loading only needed content.
  • Makes iteration faster by focusing on smaller units.
  • Enables structured level design and transitions.
Key Takeaway

Scenes scope which objects exist together; plan scenes to isolate unrelated functionality for performance and clarity.

Example
Main Menu Scene

Contains UI canvas, menu scripts, and a camera. No level geometry or enemies.

Level1 Scene

Contains terrain, player spawn, enemies, and lighting relevant to the first level.

Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to add a developed scene to Build Settings so it’s omitted from the final build.
  • Keeping unrelated systems in the same scene, making iteration slower.
Try this

Create a new scene, place a camera and a light, save as Level_Test.unity, then open Build Settings and note whether it appears in Scenes In Build.

Reflect

Which parts of your current project could be split into separate scenes to speed up iteration?

screens.title: Create, Save, and Load Scenes
screens.subtitle: Editor steps and programmatic loading for scene transitions

narration.text: Creating, saving, and loading scenes is a routine workflow that controls level flow in your game. In the editor you create a new scene with File → New Scene and save it using File → Save Scene As to produce a. unity file in your Assets. To make sure a scene is included in your final build, add it to File → Build Settings → Scenes In Build. Programmatically, transitions between scenes typically use SceneManager. LoadScene from the UnityEngine. SceneManagement namespace to load a named or indexed scene. A common misconception is that saving a scene anywhere on disk automatically includes it in builds; you must explicitly add scenes to Build Settings. Another useful technique is additive loading for larger projects where separate scenes hold distinct systems. For example, you might load a UI scene additively so its canvases persist while swapping level scenes underneath. In practice, your lab will have you create a scene named CollectibleScene, configure a simple collectible object, save the scene, add it to the build list, and test switching between scenes. Consider how you will structure scene names and indices to make code-based loading robust across team members.

keyIdea.title: Scene workflow
keyIdea.text: Create and save scenes as .unity files and use SceneManager.LoadScene plus Build Settings to control runtime transitions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Create, Save, and Load Scenes
Steps
  1. Create a new scene: File → New Scene.
  2. Save the scene: File → Save Scene As... and name it, e.g., CollectibleScene.unity.
  3. Open File → Build Settings and add scenes to Scenes In Build to include them in builds.
  4. Load scenes at runtime using SceneManager.LoadScene with the scene name or index.
Additive loading note

Load multiple scenes together when you want persistent UI or separate lighting/environment layers without merging everything into one scene.

Example code (visual)
// Example usage: load scene by name
using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;
...
SceneManager.LoadScene("Level1");
// Or load additive
SceneManager.LoadScene("UI_Scene", LoadSceneMode.Additive);
Try this

Create CollectibleScene, save it, and add it to Build Settings. Then call LoadScene by name from a simple UI button script to switch to it.

Misconception

Saving a file does not automatically include it in builds; Build Settings is the gatekeeper for packaging scenes.

screens.title: What is a Prefab?
screens.subtitle: Prefab assets as templates for reusable GameObjects

narration.text: A Prefab is an asset that stores a configured GameObject or hierarchy so you can instantiate consistent copies across scenes. Rather than recreating the same object many times, you make one authoritative template and place instances where needed. For instance, build one streetlight GameObject with a pole, a light component, a material, and an interaction script; drag it into a Prefabs folder and that becomes the Prefab asset. Any instance placed in a scene remains linked to that asset. If you change the Prefab asset, all instances update automatically — a powerful feature for sweeping design changes. Prefabs also support local overrides, where you vary a property on a single instance, like rotation or position, without altering the asset. A typical misconception is thinking that modifying an instance always creates a new Prefab asset. In fact, changing an instance creates an override; to update the asset you must use Apply All. You will practice converting a Coin GameObject into a Prefab, placing instances, and observing how a change to the original asset propagates across instances. What is a Prefab? means a prefab is a reusable asset template. create it by dragging a configured gameobject from the hierarchy into the project window.. In practical terms, prefab assets as templates for reusable gameobjects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefab definition
keyIdea.text: A Prefab is a reusable asset template. Create it by dragging a configured GameObject from the Hierarchy into the Project window.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a Prefab?
Definition

Prefab = Template

A Prefab asset stores a GameObject configuration so you can reuse it as many times as needed across scenes and builds.

Primary benefits
  • Reusability: author once, use many times.
  • Consistency: instances share the same base properties.
  • Efficiency: change the asset to update all instances.
Key Takeaway

Use Prefabs whenever you need multiple similar objects. They save time and keep behavior consistent across scenes.

Concrete example
Coin collectible

Create a small cylinder, set scale and rotation, add Rigidbody and trigger collider, apply a yellow material, then drag it into Prefabs to make a reusable coin asset.

Overrides explained

When you change one instance, the inspector shows overridden fields in bold. These overrides are local until you Apply All to push them to the Prefab asset.

Common mistake

Assuming an instance change creates a new Prefab. It only creates an override unless you apply it to the asset.

Pro tip

Keep a single Prefabs folder per project section to stay organized and avoid duplicate assets.

screens.title: Create a Prefab: Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: Convert a GameObject into a reusable asset and place instances

narration.text: Creating a Prefab from a configured GameObject is a simple but important step. Follow these steps and notice what the editor indicates: first, configure your GameObject in the Hierarchy exactly how you want the template to be, including child objects, components, and materials. For our lab, you will make a Coin object: set a cylinder’s transform, add a Rigidbody with Use Gravity off and Is Kinematic on, and mark the collider as a trigger. Next, create a Prefabs folder in the Project window to keep assets organized. Drag the GameObject from the Hierarchy into that Prefabs folder. You’ll see the Hierarchy entry turn blue, which means it’s now an instance linked to a Prefab asset. Now drag the Prefab asset from the Project window back into the Scene view multiple times to create instances. A common misconception is thinking you must duplicate GameObjects instead of using Prefabs; duplicates break the link to a single source. Try changing a property on the asset itself — for example increase the collider radius — and observe how all instances update immediately in the scene. This workflow demonstrates why Prefabs accelerate iteration and maintain consistency across levels.

keyIdea.title: Prefab creation flow
keyIdea.text: Configure in Hierarchy, drag to Prefabs folder to create the asset, then place instances from the Project window into scenes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Create a Prefab: Step-by-step
Step-by-step
  1. Configure GameObject in Hierarchy (children, components, material).
  2. Create Prefabs folder in Project window.
  3. Drag GameObject from Hierarchy into Prefabs folder to create the asset.
  4. Place instances in scenes by dragging the Prefab asset into the Scene view.
Editor indicators

After making a Prefab, hierarchy entries show a blue icon and bold inspector fields for overrides. This visual feedback helps track links between instances and the asset.

Concrete scenario
Coin prefab lab

Make a cylinder named Coin, set Transform to (0,0.5,0), rotate to lay flat, scale to coin size, add Rigidbody and trigger collider, then drag into Prefabs. Place several coins in the scene to create a collectible spread.

Apply change

Select the Prefab asset and change a property, then see all placed instances update immediately.

Misconception

Don't duplicate objects for mass placement. Use Prefabs to preserve a single source of truth.

screens.title: Instantiate Prefabs at Runtime
screens.subtitle: Using Instantiate to create objects during gameplay

narration.text: Instantiating Prefabs at runtime is how you spawn copies during gameplay. The core idea is simple: keep a reference to the Prefab asset, then call Instantiate at the desired position and rotation. In C# this typically looks like obtaining a public GameObject field for the Prefab, assigning the asset in the Inspector, and calling Instantiate(prefab, position, rotation); from code. A concrete example is spawning a health pack when a player reaches a checkpoint: the script calls Instantiate with the health pack Prefab at the checkpoint coordinates. A common misconception is confusing Prefab assets with instances in the scene; Instantiate creates a new instance linked to that asset at runtime, not a new asset. Another mistake is not assigning the Prefab reference before calling Instantiate, which causes a null reference error. Good practice is to test instantiation in Play mode and observe that runtime instances behave like editor-placed ones, including shared changes to scripts and components on the Prefab asset. Try the lab challenge to instantiate a collectible at runtime as a small coding task and observe how each spawned object remains linked to the Prefab asset for component updates.

keyIdea.title: Instantiate insight
keyIdea.text: Use Instantiate(prefab, position, rotation) to spawn linked instances at runtime; ensure the prefab reference is assigned in the Inspector.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Instantiate Prefabs at Runtime
Example script (visual)
// Visual example: assign prefab in Inspector and spawn at position
public class Spawner : MonoBehaviour
{
public GameObject collectiblePrefab; // assign in Inspector
void Spawn(Vector3 pos) {
Instantiate(collectiblePrefab, pos, Quaternion.identity);
}
}
When testing, ensure the collectiblePrefab field is set in the Inspector. If it’s null, calling Instantiate will throw an error. Runtime instances are linked to the asset but exist only while the game runs unless you save them back to the scene using editor scripts.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to assign the Prefab reference in the Inspector before calling Instantiate.
  • Expecting runtime instances to modify the Prefab asset automatically; they are linked but changes to a runtime instance don’t persist to the asset.
Try this

Add a Spawner script to an empty GameObject, assign your Coin Prefab in the Inspector, and call Spawn at a fixed position when pressing a test input while in Play mode.

Key Takeaway

Instantiate creates linked runtime instances. Assign references and test in Play mode to validate behavior.

narration.text: It's important to distinguish between a Prefab asset and its instances. A Prefab asset lives in the Project window and is the single source of truth for that template. Instances are the copies placed into scenes: they maintain a link to the asset but can have local changes called overrides. For example, if you rotate one streetlight instance to aim down a specific alley, that rotation becomes an override highlighted in the Inspector. If you want that rotation to be applied across every instance, select Apply All from the Overrides dropdown to push the change to the asset. Conversely, Revert All will discard local overrides and reset the instance to the asset's configuration. A common misconception is treating instances as independent clones — changes to one instance do not change the asset unless explicitly applied. Another confusion comes from expecting runtime-instantiated objects to persist edits back to the asset; runtime changes do not alter assets in the Project window. Always decide whether a change should be local (an override) or global (apply to the asset). Consider: when would you want a local tweak versus updating the Prefab asset for everyone?

keyIdea.title: Instance vs Asset
keyIdea.text: Instances can override properties locally; Apply All pushes those overrides to the asset, Revert All discards them and restores the asset values.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Prefab Instances vs Prefab Asset
Comparison
Prefab Asset (Project)

The stored template in Project. Editing this updates all instances unless they have an override for that field.

Prefab Instance (Hierarchy)

A placed copy in a scene. It links to the asset but can have local overrides visible in bold in the Inspector.

Use Apply All to promote an instance change to the asset. Use Revert All to discard instance changes and restore the asset's values on that instance.
Example
Changing collider radius

Change the collider radius on the Prefab asset and observe how all scene instances update. Change the Y-position on a single instance and decide if that override should be applied globally or reverted.

Common mistake

Applying an accidental local tweak globally can overwrite deliberate variations. Review overrides before using Apply All.

Checkpoint

Pick one instance, change a property, then practice Apply All and Revert All to observe the difference in behavior.

screens.title: Prefab Variants
screens.subtitle: Inherit from a base Prefab to create specialized templates

narration.text: Prefab Variants let you create a new Prefab that inherits from a base Prefab asset while allowing differences. This hierarchical approach saves duplication — you keep the shared structure and behavior in the base, and the variant changes only what needs to differ. For example, make a BaseEnemy Prefab with core components and behaviors, then create MeleeEnemy and RangedEnemy variants that swap weapons or tweak speeds. If you later update the BaseEnemy's movement script, both variants inherit that update unless the specific field is overridden in a variant. A common misconception is that variants are copies that break inheritance; in reality variants remain linked to the base for shared properties. Creating a variant is typically done by selecting a Prefab asset and choosing Create → Prefab Variant or dragging an instance and selecting Create Variant. Use variants when you need many similar templates that share most properties, as it keeps maintenance centralized and reduces the risk of inconsistent changes across assets. Prefab Variants means prefab variants inherit from a base prefab, enabling specialization while preserving shared updates from the parent asset.. In practical terms, inherit from a base prefab to create specialized templates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Variant insight
keyIdea.text: Prefab Variants inherit from a base Prefab, enabling specialization while preserving shared updates from the parent asset.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Prefab Variants
What it does

Specialize without duplication

Variants inherit all properties from a base Prefab but may override specific fields. They keep a link back to the parent so shared changes propagate.

When to use
  • Multiple similar enemies with small differences.
  • Item families where base stats are shared but visuals differ.
  • UI elements that share layout but differ in text or icons.
Concrete example
BaseEnemy → MeleeEnemy, RangedEnemy

The base contains movement and health. Variants swap weapons and tweak damage. Updating the base movement affects both variants automatically.

Common mistake

Overriding too many fields in variants defeats the purpose of inheritance. Keep variants focused on small differences.

Key Takeaway

Use Prefab Variants to maintain a central source of truth while allowing controlled specialization for variants.

screens.title: Lab: Create and Manage a Collectible Prefab
screens.subtitle: Step through the provided activity to build a Coin prefab and test overrides

narration.text: This lab guides you through making a collectible Prefab, placing instances, and practicing overrides. Start by creating a new scene and saving it as CollectibleScene. In the Hierarchy create a cylinder and rename it Coin. Set its Transform Position to 0, 0.5, 0, rotate it to lie flat, and scale it down to look coin-like. Add a Rigidbody component, uncheck Use Gravity, check Is Kinematic, and set the collider to be a trigger so the player can collect without physical collision. Optionally create a yellow material and assign it. Next, create a Prefabs folder in the Project window and drag Coin from the Hierarchy into that folder; the Hierarchy entry will show as a Prefab instance. Drag multiple Coin Prefab assets into the scene to populate the level. Then modify the Prefab asset directly — change collider radius or material color — and observe instances update. Finally, select one instance and change its Y-position or scale; note the Inspector highlights the override in bold. Use the Overrides dropdown to Apply All to push the change to the asset or Revert All to discard the local override. This hands-on practice teaches the lifecycle of Prefab creation, population, and controlled editing. Reflect on when you should apply changes globally versus keeping local variety.

keyIdea.title: Lab summary
keyIdea.text: Follow the steps: create scene, author Coin GameObject, make it a Prefab, place instances, then practice apply and revert to learn instance management.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Lab: Create and Manage a Collectible Prefab
Lab steps
  1. Create a new scene and save as CollectibleScene.unity.
  2. GameObject → 3D Object → Cylinder, rename to Coin, set Transform and scale.
  3. Add Rigidbody: Use Gravity unchecked, Is Kinematic checked. Set collider Is Trigger.
  4. Create a Prefabs folder, drag Coin into it to create the Prefab asset.
  5. Drag multiple Prefab assets into the scene to place instances.
  6. Modify the Prefab asset and observe instances updating. Change an instance and practice Apply All or Revert All.
Working through the lab makes the relationship between asset and instance concrete. Take time to observe inspector indicators and the Overrides dropdown so you know how to push or discard changes correctly.
Checkpoint
Test scenario

Change collider radius on the Prefab asset, then change the Y-position of one instance and use Apply All. Observe which properties change across all instances and which remain unique.

Troubleshooting

If instances don't update after editing the asset, confirm you edited the asset in the Project window and not a duplicate asset with a similar name.

Lab takeaway

This lab builds confidence with Prefab lifecycle: author, create asset, place instances, and manage overrides deliberately.

screens.title: Best Practices and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: How to stay organized and avoid pitfalls with Scenes and Prefabs

narration.text: As projects grow, small habits with Scenes and Prefabs pay dividends. First, keep a clear folder structure in the Project window — e. g., Prefabs, Scenes, Materials — so teammates can quickly find and reuse assets. Second, name scenes and prefabs consistently; descriptive names prevent accidental edits of the wrong asset. Third, limit overrides in instances: if many overrides exist, consider whether the asset should change instead. A common mistake is applying a local tweak globally without review, which can overwrite deliberate instance variations. Another pitfall is creating duplicate Prefab assets because two people exported similar templates; this fragments updates and causes inconsistency. Use Prefab Variants when you have families of related objects — variants centralize shared logic while allowing small differences. When loading scenes, remember to add them to Build Settings; forgetting this step results in missing scenes at runtime. For runtime instantiation, always ensure Prefab references are assigned in scripts to avoid null references. These practical rules reduce wasted time and keep your project maintainable as it scales. Best Practices and Common Mistakes means organize assets, use consistent names, minimize unnecessary overrides, prefer variants over duplicates, and always add required scenes to build settings.. In practical terms, how to stay organized and avoid pitfalls with scenes and prefabs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Organize assets, use consistent names, minimize unnecessary overrides, prefer variants over duplicates, and always add required scenes to Build Settings.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Best Practices and Common Mistakes
Best practices
  • Organize folders: Prefabs, Scenes, Materials, Scripts.
  • Use clear, consistent naming conventions for scenes and prefabs.
  • Prefer Prefab Variants over duplicate assets for similar objects.
  • Minimize overrides; apply to asset only when change is truly global.
Avoid

Avoid creating multiple slightly different assets when a variant or override would suffice — it increases maintenance cost.

Checklist
Scenes in build?

Confirm every playable scene is added to Build Settings before packaging the game.

Prefab references assigned?

Ensure scripts that Instantiate prefabs have their prefab fields assigned in the Inspector.

Are overrides intentional?

Review bold fields in the Inspector and decide whether to Apply All or Revert All.

Final tip

Make small, reviewable changes to Prefabs and use variants for family differences to keep projects maintainable.

narration.text: Use this quick assessment to check your understanding and reinforce practical steps. One sample question asks which asset type ensures that changes propagate to all placed enemies across scenes; the correct answer is Prefab, since it is the template linked to instances. Another asks how to include a scene in the final build — you must add it to Scenes In Build in Build Settings. Practically, try the following mini-tasks: create a scene called TestScene, add it to Build Settings, then author a small GameObject, make it a Prefab, place two instances, change a property on the asset and observe instance updates, then change one instance and practice Apply All and Revert All. Reflect on misconceptions you encountered and document one instance where you applied an override intentionally versus when you applied a change to the asset. These reflective tasks are important because understanding the distinction between local instance edits and global asset edits saves a lot of debugging time in larger projects. End by asking: which changes in my current project should be made at the asset level and which should remain instance-specific?

narration.text: These are the essential definitions to remember. A Scene is a container saved as a. unity file that holds GameObjects, cameras, lights, and environment for a level or UI state. The SceneManager class is the runtime A P I you use to load and unload scenes programmatically. Build Settings contains the Scenes In Build list — only scenes here are included in a packaged game. Finally, a Prefab is a reusable asset template in the Project window that stores a configured GameObject or hierarchy. Memorize these concise definitions so that when you design levels or write code you know which concept controls structure, packaging, and reuse. Ask yourself: which scene should hold persistent UI versus per-level geometry? That decision will shape how you load and organize content. Key Concepts — Part 1 means scene = .unity container; scenemanager = api to load/unload; build settings = scenes included in builds; prefab = reusable gameobject asset.. In practical terms, short definitions you should recall quickly. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Scene = .unity container; SceneManager = API to load/unload; Build Settings = scenes included in builds; Prefab = reusable GameObject asset.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Scene
A .unity file that contains all objects for a level or UI state.
SceneManager
API used to load and unload scenes programmatically at runtime.
Build Settings
Window where you add scenes to include them in the final build packaging.
Summary

These four concepts form the structural backbone of scene and build management. Keep them in mind when organizing levels and code-driven transitions.

narration.text: These final key concepts focus on Prefabs and instance management. A Prefab is a reusable template stored in the Project window and becomes the authoritative asset for copies placed in scenes. A Prefab Instance is a scene copy that retains a link back to that asset. Overrides are local instance changes highlighted in bold in the Inspector; they let you vary individual instances without changing the asset. Use Apply All to push overrides from an instance back to the asset so all instances inherit the change, or Revert All to discard instance-only changes and restore the asset values. Prefab Variants inherit from a base Prefab, allowing specialized templates that still receive shared updates. These concepts enable consistent content, faster iteration, and scalable asset management. As a quick takeaway, decide for a change whether it should be global (apply to the asset) or local (stay as an override). That decision keeps collaboration and iteration predictable.

keyIdea.title: Prefab essentials
keyIdea.text: Prefab asset = template. Instance = linked copy. Overrides = local edits. Apply/Revert control propagation. Variants = inherited specializations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts — Part 2
Prefab
An asset template in Project used to create consistent GameObjects across scenes.
Overrides
Local instance changes that differ from the Prefab asset; shown in bold in the Inspector.
Prefab Variant
A specialized Prefab that inherits from a base Prefab and can override specific fields while keeping shared updates.
Final takeaway

Decide deliberately whether a change belongs on the asset (global) or an instance (local). That choice keeps collaboration and iteration predictable and reduces bugs.
